Let's dive into Chapter 8: Finishing Strong—Overcoming the Final Surge of Resistance.
You know that feeling when you're almost done with a big project, but suddenly, doubts creep in? Maybe you start second-guessing every detail, or you get the urge to just walk away and leave it unfinished. That’s the final surge of resistance showing up, and it usually hits hardest right before the finish line. Why does this happen? Well, finishing means putting your work out there for everyone to see. It means you’re open to judgment, feedback, or—sometimes—the dreaded silence. The stakes feel higher, and resistance is quick to step in, trying to shield you from possible disappointment.
Here’s something to pay attention to: the last stretch of a project is often the toughest. Not because the work itself is suddenly harder, but because resistance is fighting with everything it’s got to keep things exactly the way they are. You might be tempted to keep tweaking, delay your deadline, or even start something new just to avoid finishing. So, how do you push through this last hurdle? First, set a clear finish line. Define exactly what “done” looks like for you, and promise yourself you’ll get there. Second, limit those last-minute changes. It’s easy to get caught up in making endless tweaks, but sometimes, good enough really is enough. Third, enlist some accountability. Tell a friend, a colleague, or even your audience when you plan to finish. That little bit of outside support can make a world of difference. And finally, picture yourself crossing that finish line. Imagine the relief, the pride, and the satisfaction you’ll feel once it’s done. Let that vision overpower any hesitation.
Think of it like running a marathon. That final mile? It’s not longer than the rest, but with tired legs and a tired mind, it feels like the hardest. The trick is to keep moving—one step, then the next—focusing on progress instead of the pain.
In the end, finishing is all about courage. You’re letting go, trusting that your work is ready to stand on its own. And when you push through that last wave of resistance, you don’t just complete a project—you bring something new into the world.
